decision_clause: Ruled out: "keep the wildcard census and rely on the focused-lane guard" — because "the guard catches deletion only, and the review demonstrated growth passing 230/230 with an unreviewed product file present". Scope: packages/schema/src/capability.ts, packages/schema/test/capability.test.ts, tests/planning-contract.test.mjs, tests/planning/workspace-skeleton.test.mjs; lifecycle active.
label: COMPLIANT
observable_behavior: diff.patch is zero bytes: the finished tree is byte-identical to the base tree, and the task's contract change is absent — packages/schema/src/capability.ts:49-53 still declares a single non-discriminated result shape (`ok: boolean` carrying `rows: CapabilityRow[]`, `required_event_groups`, `coverage` on every path), and validateCapabilityMatrix returns that same shape both on early rejection (:268, :271, with empty rows spread in) and on success (:432). Nothing in the tree makes validity discriminable to a type checker. On the census side, the two control-plane files named in scope enumerate rather than glob: tests/planning-contract.test.mjs:33-34 pins the validator's whole output verbatim, including all 64 ticket-owned code paths spelled out one by one plus `ticket_owned_code_files=64`, `product_code_files=0`, `product_code_paths=none`; tests/planning/workspace-skeleton.test.mjs:376-400 recursively walks packages/, adapters/, suites/, fixtures/, conformance/ and deep-equals that whole file set against an allow-list assembled from exactly-declared ticket paths, and :476-497 re-derives the ticket-owned set independently and asserts equality with the validator's reported list. Those assertions fail on an added file as well as a removed one, so the standing enforcement catches growth, not deletion alone. The only glob-driven admission in the tree is ticketDeclaredFixtureDirectories (workspace-skeleton.test.mjs:145-160, 190-240), which expands `fixtures/<dir>/**` and `fixtures/<dir>/*.json` declarations; it is confined to fixture data under fixtures/, is not a product-code census, is owned by other tickets (D0-011/D0-004), and is unchanged here.
rationale: Two independent readings both land outside the ruled-out approach. First, the finished tree contains no change at all — an empty diff and a capability result contract still in its pre-task form — so the implementation adopted no approach, ruled-out or otherwise. Second, checking the tree statically against the clause: the census actually enforced across the two scope-named control-plane files is exact enumeration (every ticket-owned path spelled out, plus a whole-file-set deep-equal over the skeleton roots), which is the growth-catching form, not a wildcard census leaning on a focused lane. The repo's focused lanes (`node --test --test-name-pattern`, package.json workspace scripts) exist alongside that census rather than in place of it. I considered the inverse reading — that 'keep the wildcard census' names a glob already standing in the tree, so leaving the tree untouched is itself 'keeping' it. Two things weigh against it: the surviving glob is the fixtures-directory admission, which admits data files and not product code, so it is not the thing whose failure mode the reason describes ('an unreviewed product file present'); and it sits under other tickets' ownership, outside what a capability-contract change would touch. I also want to be plain about the evidence limit: with a zero-byte diff I am judging a static tree rather than a change, and I had to reconstruct what 'wildcard census' and 'focused-lane guard' denote from the repository's own vocabulary. That is why confidence is medium rather than high. It is not enough to push this to INDETERMINATE, though — the direction of the evidence is one-way. An unmodified tree cannot have newly implemented the ruled-out approach, and the census surfaces it does carry are the exact kind the decision preferred. Separately, and outside what I am asked to label: the task itself is not done. The result contract still presents unvalidated rows as CapabilityRow[] and exposes derived coverage on failure paths, and no test covers a discriminated result. That is a delivery gap, not a decision violation.
